nodes.example_from_source: traffic, bounce rate, conversion, CTR, time on page; clickbait causes high bounce
nodes.teaching_note: Online businesses capture every click. Core digital metrics: website traffic (by source — direct/organic/paid/social/referral); bounce rate (% leaving after one page — high = poor experience, irrelevant traffic, clickbait, or slow load); conversion rate (% completing the desired action); click-through rate (CTR); average time on page; page views per visit. Used for performance assessment, user-behaviour understanding, customer-journey mapping and resource allocation (spend more where traffic CONVERTS, not just where it's high).

distractors.why: purchases would LOWER bounce; high bounce signals irrelevant content/slow load

distractors.wrong: A low number of page views being irrelevant
distractors.why: the issue is content relevance/experience driving people away, i.e. high bounce

nodes.sample_question: A site gets huge traffic but a high bounce rate and low time-on-page. The most likely causes include slow load time, high prices, and ____.
nodes.failure_mode: Optimising for raw traffic (a vanity metric) instead of conversion; ignoring bounce rate as a quality signal.

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.formula: CLV = ARPU / churn rate ; ROAS = revenue/ad spend ; inventory turnover = COGS/avg inventory ; conversion = purchases/visitors

variables.churn rate: fraction of customers lost per period

nodes.example_from_source: $15/0.02=$750; ROAS 125%; inv turnover 4.44x; conversion 2%; RevPAR Rs1400
nodes.teaching_note: Key formulas from the lecture: CLV (subscription) = ARPU ÷ churn rate (e.g. $15/0.02 = $750; if churn rises to 3%, $15/0.03 = $500 — a 1pp churn rise cuts LTV by $250). ROAS = revenue ÷ ad spend (500 sales × $250 = $125,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.25 = 125%). Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ average inventory (avg = (500k+400k)/2 = 450k; $2M/450k = 4.44×). Conversion rate = purchases ÷ visitors (300/15,000 = 2%; to reach 5% needs 750 sales, i.e. 450 more). RevPAR (OYO) = ADR × occupancy (₹2,000 × 70% = ₹1,400).

distractors.why: CLV divides ARPU by churn; it does not multiply ARPU by churn
$500 corresponds to a 3% churn rate; at 2% it is $15/0.02 = $750

nodes.sample_question: A subscription service has ARPU of $15/month and a monthly churn rate of 2%. What is the customer lifetime value?
nodes.failure_mode: Multiplying instead of dividing by churn, or forgetting CLV = ARPU/churn (higher churn → lower CLV).

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.concept: Creator economy & the creator business lifecycle
nodes.example_from_source: YouTube/Patreon/Substack; Bhuvan Bam, Graphy; 4-stage lifecycle
nodes.teaching_note: The creator economy lets independent creators (bloggers, YouTubers, streamers, artisans) monetise content/products directly via platforms (YouTube, TikTok, Patreon, Substack), bypassing traditional gatekeepers (publishers, labels). The creator business has four lifecycle stages: CREATION (turn talent into consumable content/product) → DISCOVERY (build audience/community on social platforms) → MONETISATION (convert audience into paying customers — timing matters: too early loses interest, too late earns nothing) → GROWTH (end-to-end management: finance, CRM, analytics). Monetisation methods: ads/revenue-share, brand sponsorships, subscriptions/tips, creator-led commerce, courses, NFTs/social tokens.

distractors.why: discovery is building the audience; turning it into paying customers is monetisation
creation is making the content; revenue conversion is monetisation

nodes.sample_question: In the creator business lifecycle, the stage of converting an engaged audience into paying customers is called ____.
nodes.failure_mode: Collapsing discovery and monetisation — building an audience (discovery) is distinct from converting it to revenue (monetisation).

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.example_from_source: 80-20 creator earnings; creator↔fan two-sided network effect
nodes.teaching_note: Creator-economy startups (creator tools/SaaS, fan subscriptions, creator commerce, brand collaborations) track: ARR/MRR, CAC, LTV, conversion of audience→paid subscribers, creator earnings, creator retention, and engagement (likes/comments/shares). The 80-20 RULE applies: the top ~20% of creators drive ~80% of earnings — so platforms must ensure enough creators earn a minimum to stay (retention), since a two-sided creator↔fan network effect/flywheel powers growth. Creator acquisition is expensive, so loyalty compounds.

distractors.why: the network effect is value rising with users; the earnings concentration is the 80-20 rule
churn is users leaving; this is about skewed earnings distribution (80-20)

nodes.sample_question: On creator platforms, the top ~20% of creators drive about ~80% of total earnings. This concentration is known as the ____.
nodes.failure_mode: Ignoring the long tail — assuming earnings are evenly spread when ~20% of creators capture ~80%.

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.example_from_source: library/town-square analogies; coffee supply chain; consensus of nodes
nodes.teaching_note: A blockchain is a decentralised, distributed digital ledger held in many identical copies across a network. Data is grouped into blocks chained cryptographically to the previous block; an entry cannot be altered without changing all subsequent blocks AND winning consensus of the majority of nodes — making it tamper-evident/immutable. Three pillars: TRUST (everyone can verify), SECURITY (cryptographic linkage, hard to hack), DECENTRALISATION (no single owner — like a community garden). Uses far beyond currency: supply-chain tracking, real estate titles, voting, healthcare records.

distractors.why: decentralisation = no single controller; not-changeable-once-added is immutability
anonymity concerns identity; tamper-resistance of recorded data is immutability

nodes.sample_question: Which property of blockchain means that once data is added it is practically impossible to change without detection?
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing immutability (can't be altered undetected) with decentralisation (no central authority) — both are blockchain traits but distinct.

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.example_from_source: 1991 Haber/Stornetta concept; 2009 Bitcoin (Nakamoto); Ethereum smart contracts
nodes.teaching_note: They are NOT the same. Blockchain is the underlying technology (concept outlined 1991 by Haber & Stornetta for tamper-proof timestamps). Bitcoin is ONE application of blockchain — a cryptocurrency/peer-to-peer electronic cash system introduced by Satoshi Nakamoto in 2008/2009, with no trusted third party. Bitcoin uses blockchain to record payments, but blockchain powers thousands of other uses (supply chain, voting, smart contracts). Blockchain vs banking: 24/7 vs business hours, user-set vs fixed fees, no mandatory KYC, harder for governments to seize.

distractors.wrong: Bitcoin and blockchain are the same thing
distractors.why: blockchain is the underlying tech; Bitcoin is just one cryptocurrency built on it
Ethereum is a programmable blockchain platform, not a physical coin

nodes.sample_question: A developer picks Ethereum over Bitcoin because it supports smart contracts and decentralised apps, not just payments. What does this show about the blockchain-vs-Bitcoin relationship?
nodes.failure_mode: Treating 'blockchain' and 'Bitcoin' as synonyms — blockchain is the technology; Bitcoin is one currency application of it.

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.example_from_source: rental door-code example; real estate title transfer; Ethereum
nodes.teaching_note: A smart contract is computer code embedded in a blockchain that automatically executes the terms of an agreement when predefined conditions are met — no intermediary required (e.g. a rental smart contract releases the door code when the deposit is paid, and disables it if rent is unpaid). Popularised by Ethereum. Used in real-estate title transfer, supply chain and decentralised finance. Benefits: removes middlemen, speeds execution, increases transparency and reduces fraud.

distractors.why: an NFT proves ownership of a unique asset; a smart contract is self-executing agreement code
a wallet stores keys/coins; a smart contract executes agreement logic

nodes.sample_question: Code on a blockchain that automatically transfers a property title once payment conditions are met, with no intermediary, is called a ____.
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing a smart contract (self-executing code) with an NFT (proof of ownership of a unique asset).

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.example_from_source: Beeple $69.3M Christie's, NBA Top Shot, Decentraland, Gucci virtual sneakers
nodes.teaching_note: An NFT is a blockchain-based token that represents verifiable ownership and authenticity of a UNIQUE digital (or digital-twin) item — even when identical copies exist anywhere. 'Non-fungible' = unique/not interchangeable (unlike a Bitcoin, which is fungible). Built largely on Ethereum (CryptoKitties were early). Applications: digital art (Beeple sold for ~$69.3M at Christie's), collectibles (NBA Top Shot), virtual real estate (Decentraland), music/royalties, gaming items, fashion (Gucci virtual sneakers). Lets creators prove originality and capture value/royalties.

distractors.why: an NFT proves ownership/authenticity; it does not police copyright globally
it establishes ownership/authenticity of the original token, not all copies

nodes.sample_question: A digital artist wants to prove she is the original creator of an artwork that thousands have copied online. What does an NFT establish for her?
nodes.failure_mode: Thinking an NFT prevents copying or grants copyright — it proves authenticity/ownership of the original, it doesn't stop copies.

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.example_from_source: Bitcoin/Ethereum/Ripple/Litecoin; volatility, irreversibility, regulation risks
nodes.teaching_note: A digital/virtual currency secured by cryptography, operating on a decentralised blockchain with no central bank. Types: Bitcoin (first/largest, 'digital gold'), Ethereum (smart contracts/dApps), Ripple/XRP (payments), Litecoin ('silver'), Bitcoin Cash, Cardano/Polkadot. Uses: transactions, investment, cross-border remittance, fundraising (ICOs), privacy (Monero), smart contracts/DeFi. Benefits: security, decentralisation, transparency, low fees, financial inclusion. Risks: VOLATILITY, regulatory bans, hacked exchanges/wallets, IRREVERSIBILITY (no chargebacks), environmental cost of mining.

distractors.why: crypto is highly volatile; stability is not a feature
transactions are irreversible with no central authority to refund

nodes.sample_question: Which of these is a key RISK (not benefit) of holding cryptocurrency?
nodes.failure_mode: Listing only benefits and ignoring risks (volatility, irreversibility, regulation, security) — or vice versa.

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.example_from_source: 21M cap, Satoshi divisibility, digital gold, El Salvador legal tender
nodes.teaching_note: Bitcoin (Satoshi Nakamoto, 2008 white paper 'A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System') is a decentralised digital currency with no central bank. Characteristics: decentralised; LIMITED SUPPLY capped at 21 million (vs fiat which governments can print, causing devaluation); pseudonymous (addresses not directly tied to identities); immutable transactions; divisible to the smallest unit (Satoshi = 1/100,000,000 BTC). Used two ways: as alternative currency, or as a 'digital gold' store of value. El Salvador made it legal tender (2021); Japan recognised it (2017).

distractors.wrong: Unlimited supply set by a central bank
distractors.why: Bitcoin has no central bank and a fixed 21M cap
Bitcoin is not gold-backed; its scarcity comes from the protocol's 21M cap

nodes.sample_question: What feature of Bitcoin — a hard cap of 21 million coins — distinguishes it from fiat currencies like the rupee?
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming Bitcoin's supply can be expanded like fiat — it is capped at 21M, which underpins the 'digital gold' scarcity argument.

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.example_from_source: 1.0 static (LiveJournal), 2.0 social (Facebook/YouTube), 3.0 decentralised (Ethereum/ChatGPT)
nodes.teaching_note: Web 1.0 (read-only/static): one-way information, minimal interaction, company-published pages (early MySpace, LiveJournal). Web 2.0 (read-write/social): user-generated content, interactivity, social platforms and APIs (Facebook, YouTube, Wikipedia) — centralised data control by corporations. Web 3.0 (read-write-execute/semantic): AI-driven, machine-understandable, DECENTRALISED data and ownership, blockchain, VR/AR, personalisation (Ethereum dApps, ChatGPT, Decentraland). Business shift: from online presence (1.0) to engagement (2.0) to decentralised models + data privacy + AI (3.0).

distractors.why: Web 3.0 is decentralised/semantic/AI-driven; centralised social UGC is Web 2.0
Web 1.0 is static read-only; user-generated social content is Web 2.0

nodes.sample_question: A read-write social web where users create content on centralised platforms like Facebook and YouTube describes which stage of the web?
nodes.failure_mode: Mixing the stages — read-only=1.0, read-write/social=2.0, decentralised/semantic=3.0.

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.concept: AI / ML / Deep Learning / Generative AI / LLM / Agentic AI
nodes.example_from_source: AI⊃ML⊃DL⊃GenAI⊃LLM; Gmail spam (ML); ChatGPT (GenAI); agentic flight-booking
nodes.teaching_note: Nested hierarchy: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (machines mimicking human intelligence, incl. rule-based systems) ⊃ MACHINE LEARNING (learns patterns from data, improves with experience — e.g. Gmail spam filter) ⊃ DEEP LEARNING (neural networks for in-depth pattern extraction) ⊃ GENERATIVE AI (creates new content — text/image/audio/code; ChatGPT, DALL·E) ⊃ LLMs (large language models trained on vast text — GPT-4o, Claude, Llama). AGENTIC AI is the newest frontier: independent agents that plan and perform multi-step tasks WITHOUT step-by-step prompting (e.g. autonomously book/reschedule/refund a flight), unlike generative AI which responds to prompts.

distractors.why: generative AI creates content from prompts; autonomous multi-step action is agentic AI
ML learns patterns from data; autonomous goal-directed action is agentic AI

nodes.sample_question: AI that acts as an independent agent — planning and executing multi-step tasks (e.g. booking and rescheduling a flight) without being prompted at each step — is called ____.
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing generative AI (creates content in response to prompts) with agentic AI (autonomously plans and acts).

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.example_from_source: ONDC = open network like UPI; buyer app <-> gateway <-> seller app; not a platform
nodes.teaching_note: ONDC (Open Network for Digital Commerce) is a Government-of-India digital-public-infrastructure initiative (like UPI) that democratises e-commerce. It is NOT a platform/app and NOT a regulator — it is an OPEN, decentralised, unbundled, INTEROPERABLE PROTOCOL. Closed platform-centric e-commerce (Amazon/Flipkart) locks a buyer to that app's sellers; ONDC's open network lets a buyer on any buyer-app transact with sellers registered via any seller-app, via the ONDC gateway. It removes the central intermediary, attacks platform lock-in, high commissions (Swiggy/Zomato 23-27%), and seller data-capture.

distractors.why: ONDC is the open network; platforms like Amazon/Flipkart are the closed model it contrasts with
ONDC explicitly is neither a regulator nor a marketplace app — it is an open protocol

nodes.sample_question: ONDC lets a buyer on one app purchase from a seller registered on a different app, with no central intermediary owning the transaction. This makes ONDC a ____, not a ____.
nodes.failure_mode: Calling ONDC a 'platform' or an 'app' or a 'regulator' — it is an open interoperable network/protocol, analogous to UPI.

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.example_from_source: 5 pillars; Vijay atta flow (Gupta Kirana vs Big Basket; Dunzo vs Good Box)
nodes.teaching_note: ONDC's unbundled architecture has FIVE pillars: (1) buyer-side apps (Paytm, WhatsApp — demand side); (2) seller-side apps (Flipkart, Big Basket, kirana stores — supply side); (3) adapter interfaces (open APIs/backend protocol); (4) gateway (discoverability — multicasts a buyer's search to seller apps); (5) open registries (lists of participants, network policies). Transaction flow (Vijay buying atta): buyer-app search → gateway multicasts to seller nodes via registry → results (e.g. Gupta Kirana ₹50 vs Big Basket ₹150) → choose seller → search logistics (Dunzo ₹50 vs Good Box ₹70) → choose delivery → pay via UPI/COD. Roles unbundled: buyer app, seller app, logistics buyer/seller apps, gateway, registry, tech/payment providers.

distractors.why: the registry lists participants and policies; the gateway multicasts searches for discovery
the seller app lets sellers list; the gateway routes/multicasts the buyer's search

nodes.sample_question: In ONDC, the component that takes a buyer's search request and multicasts it to relevant seller apps to enable discovery is the ____.
nodes.failure_mode: Confusing the gateway (discovery/multicasting) with the registry (lists of participants/policies).

nodes.subject: NABM
nodes.example_from_source: seller discoverability + one registration + autonomy + no 23-27% cut; liability/ownership challenge
nodes.teaching_note: Benefits: BUYERS get a single point of access to all domains/sellers, wider price options and hyper-local fulfilment; SELLERS become discoverable to the whole buyer universe with ONE registration, gain autonomy (less dependence on one platform's rules), and avoid heavy platform commissions (saving the 23-27% food-delivery cut); TECH companies can monetise unbundled services (payments, logistics, cataloguing) quickly. Challenges: incentive to switch (early adoption), digital hand-holding/onboarding of small sellers, OWNERSHIP OF TRANSACTIONS (who is liable for a damaged/ wrong order — seller? logistics? buyer app?), conflict resolution, and data privacy/ownership.

distractors.wrong: By guaranteeing the highest price for goods
distractors.why: ONDC widens access/competition and cuts commissions; it does not guarantee high prices

distractors.wrong: By acting as the single platform that owns the customer
distractors.why: ONDC is the opposite — an open network that removes single-platform ownership/lock-in

nodes.sample_question: A small kirana store dislikes paying a large platform commission and being bound by one platform's rules. How does ONDC primarily help it?
nodes.failure_mode: Assuming ONDC is friction-free — its hard problems are transaction ownership/liability, onboarding incentives and data governance.
